claims.source: Indeed, many intracellular bacterial pathogens hijack or alter normal PTMs of host proteins to manipulate cells and promote their pathogenesis (Roy and Mukherjee, 2009; Patel et al., 2009; Fiskin et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Roy and Mukherjee, 2009; Patel et al., 2009; Fiskin et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Selective autophagy is predominantly regulated by PTMs rather than transcription.
claims.source: Selective autophagy is predominantly regulated by PTMs rather than transcription (Lamark et al., 2017), as it is under the control of several types of modification, especially ubiquitylation and phosphorylation (Herhaus and Dikic, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lamark et al., 2017 and Herhaus and Dikic, 2015.

claims.claim: Initial targeting of intracellular structures to autophagy is mediated by ubiquitylation of the cargo.
claims.source: Initial targeting of intracellular structures (intracellular pathogens, damaged organelles, protein aggregates, etc.) to autophagy is mediated by ubiquitylation of the cargo.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of selective autophagy, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Autophagy receptors recognize ubiquitin signals and recruit phagophore membranes to the cargo via interactions with LC3/GABARAP proteins.
claims.source: Autophagy receptors then recognize these ubiquitin signals and recruit phagophore membranes to the cargo via interactions with LC3/GABARAP proteins embedded in these vesicles, ultimately enveloping cargo inside a continuous autophagic vacuole competent for fusion with lysosomes.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the mechanism of selective autophagy, drawing from established knowledge in the field.

claims.claim: Ubiquitylation of p62 and phosphorylation of Optineurin increase their activity upon recruitment to cargo, forming a positive feedback loop promoting autophagosome completion.
claims.source: For example, ubiquitylation of p62 and phosphorylation of Optineurin increase their activity upon recruitment to cargo, forming a positive feedback loop promoting autophagosome completion (Peng et al., 2017; Matsumoto et al., 2011; Heo et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2017; Matsumoto et al., 2011; Heo et al., 2015.

claims.claim: Some ubiquitin ligases required for selective autophagy of Mtb have been identified.
claims.source: In the case of Mtb, some ubiquitin ligases required for selective autophagy have been identified (Manzanillo et al., 2013; Franco et al., 2017), but their substrates and roles are still mysterious and other ubiquitin ligases are likely required.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Manzanillo et al., 2013 and Franco et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Some autophagy receptors have been implicated in autophagy of the Mtb-containing vacuole.
claims.source: Likewise, some autophagy receptors have been implicated in autophagy of the Mtb-containing vacuole (Watson et al., 2012; Manzanillo et al., 2013; Franco et al., 2017), but many have not been tested (Rogov et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Watson et al., 2012; Manzanillo et al., 2013; Franco et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The study used mass spectrometry to comprehensively identify changes in host protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during a 24 hr time course of primary murine macrophages infected with virulent Mtb.
claims.source: Here, we report our findings using mass spectrometry (MS) to comprehensively identify changes in host protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during a 24 hr time course of primary murine macrophages infected with virulent Mtb.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach used in the study.

claims.claim: The study identified hundreds of dynamically regulated phosphorylation and ubiquitylation sites during Mtb infection.
claims.source: We identified hundreds of dynamically regulated phosphorylation and ubiquitylation sites, indicating that dramatic remodeling of multiple host pathways, both expected and unexpected, occurred during infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the mass spectrometry data generated in the study.

claims.claim: Most of the cellular changes during Mtb infection were not captured by mRNA profiling.
claims.source: Most of these cellular changes were not captured by mRNA profiling, and included activation of ubiquitin-mediated autophagy, an evolutionarily ancient cellular antimicrobial system.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of the proteomic data with transcriptomic data, as shown in Figure 1D-F.

claims.claim: The analysis revealed that TAX1BP1 mediates clearance of ubiquitylated Mtb and targets bacteria to LC3-positive phagophores.
claims.source: This analysis also revealed that a particular autophagy receptor, TAX1BP1, mediates clearance of ubiquitylated Mtb and targets bacteria to LC3-positive phagophores.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the genetic and microscopy experiments shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: Primary murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages were infected with Mtb in biological triplicate and harvested at 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-, and 24 hr post-infection.
claims.source: To this end, we infected primary murine bone-marrow-derived macrophages with Mtb in biological triplicate, harvested infected cells at 2-, 4-, 6-, 8-, and 24 hr post-infection, and prepared protein lysates (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design, as shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Time-matched mock infections were performed at 0 hr, 6 hr, and 24 hr time points.
claims.source: We also performed time-matched mock infections of the same macrophages harvested at an early (0 hr), middle (6 hr), or late (24 hr) time points.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claims.claim: Extremely few changes were identified between uninfected cells at all three time points (0, 6, and 24 hr).
claims.source: Because we identified extremely few changes between uninfected cells at all three time points, we simply matched the Mtb-infected cell data from the 2- and 4 hr time points with the data from the 0 hr mock sample, and the 6- and 8 hr time points with the data from the 6 hr mock sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C.

claims.claim: Pair-wise comparison of parent ion MS intensity measurements between technical and biological replicates from the same condition were highly reproducible.
claims.source: Pair-wise comparison of parent ion MS intensity measurements between technical and biological replicates from the same condition were highly reproducible, as indicated by strong correlation coefficients from global abundance, phospho-enriched, or diGly-enriched samples (Supplementary file 1; Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claims.claim: Over 1000 statistically significant changes in abundance or PTMs were identified during Mtb infection.
claims.source: Comparison of peptide levels in Mtb infected samples versus uninfected controls revealed over 1000 statistically significant changes in abundance or PTMs during Mtb infection (Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3; Figure 2C-G), indicating pronounced changes to the macrophage proteome.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplements 2–3 and Figure 2C-G.

claims.claim: The number of statistically significant changes in protein abundance or ubiquitylation progressively increased over the time course.
claims.source: The number of statistically significant changes in protein abundance or ubiquitylation progressively increased over the time course (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: Phosphopeptide changes were bimodal with the greatest number of changes occurring early (2- or 4 hr post-infection) or late (24 hr) after Mtb infection.
claims.source: In contrast, phosphopeptide changes were bimodal with the greatest number of phosphopeptide changes occurring early (2- or 4 hr post-infection) or late (24 hr) after Mtb infection (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: At 6 hr post-infection, there was weak correlation (ρ = 0.36) between relative protein and RNA abundance.
claims.source: Overall, our data is consistent with previous findings of dendritic cells treated with LPS (Berg-Larsen et al., 2013), as we observed weak correlation between relative protein and RNA abundance early after infection (6 hr time point, Pearson coefficient ρ = 0.36, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), but at 24 hr post-infection the correlation was much stronger (ρ = 0.74, Figure 1D) indicating that by this time point the changes in the proteome are largely reflective of changes in the transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4, and is supported by citation to Berg-Larsen et al., 2013.

claims.claim: At 24 hr post-infection, the correlation between relative protein and RNA abundance was much stronger (ρ = 0.74).
claims.source: Overall, our data is consistent with previous findings of dendritic cells treated with LPS (Berg-Larsen et al., 2013), as we observed weak correlation between relative protein and RNA abundance early after infection (6 hr time point, Pearson coefficient ρ = 0.36, Figure 1—figure supplement 4), but at 24 hr post-infection the correlation was much stronger (ρ = 0.74, Figure 1D) indicating that by this time point the changes in the proteome are largely reflective of changes in the transcriptome.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Poor correlations were observed between relative changes in mRNA compared to changes in phosphorylated (ρ = 0.37) or ubiquitylated proteins (ρ = 0.52) at 24 hr post-infection.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed poor correlations between relative changes in mRNA compared to changes in phosphorylated (ρ = 0.37, Figure 1E) or ubiquitylated proteins (ρ = 0.52, Figure 1F) at this same late time point.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the correlation analysis shown in Figure 1E and 1F.

claims.claim: Changes in RNA abundance is a moderate predictor for changes in protein abundance in response to infection, but other biological processes controlled by PTMs are at play during macrophage infection.
claims.source: Thus, these results suggest that while changes in RNA abundance is a moderate predictor for changes in protein abundance in response to infection, other biological process controlled by PTMs are at play during macrophage infection, reinforcing the notion that proteomics is a valuable method to identify biological processes during infection that are independent of gene expression.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claims.claim: 470 proteins changed significantly in abundance during Mtb infection.
claims.source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: 1489 proteins changed significantly in phosphorylation during Mtb infection.
claims.source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: 606 proteins changed significantly in ubiquitylation during Mtb infection.
claims.source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: There was limited overlap between proteins that changed in abundance, phosphorylation, or ubiquitylation during Mtb infection.
claims.source: A comparison of individual proteins that changed significantly in abundance (n = 470), phosphorylation (n = 1489), or ubiquitylation (n = 606) during Mtb infection, indicated limited overlap between the three categories (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the Venn diagram shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Antiviral responses were highly enriched in the global abundance dataset (p=4.53×10−20).
claims.source: As expected based on previous literature, antiviral responses were highly enriched (p=4.53×10−20 in the global abundance dataset; Figure 3C), including response to type I (IFN-β p=4.25×10−16, and IFN-α 3.81 × 10−10 in the global abundance dataset; Figure 3C), likely due to phagosome perforation and activation of the cGAS/STING/TBK1 pathway (Flynn et al., 1993; Cooper et al., 1993; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C, and is supported by citations to Flynn et al., 1993; Cooper et al., 1993; Moreira-Teixeira et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Small GTPase mediated signal transduction was highly enriched in the phosphopeptide datasets (p=2.12×10−26).
claims.source: Small GTPase mediated signal transduction was also highly enriched in the phosphopeptide datasets, which included Rab GTPases (Rab7, 8b, and 14), guanine nucleotide exchange factors (RabGef1, ArfGef1-2, ArhGef2, Dock1, 2, 5, 8, and 11), and GTPase activators (ArfGap 1, 2, 3, 12, 17, 18, 24, 25, 30, 35) (p=2.12×10−26; Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Enrichment of proteins in the category 'regulation of catabolic processes' (p=2.39×10−25) was identified in the phosphopeptide dataset.
claims.source: We identified an enrichment in modified proteins in the category 'regulation of catabolic processes' (p=2.39×10−25 in the phosphopeptide dataset; Figure 3C), which includes components of the autophagy machinery such as Atg4b, Rubicon, autophagy kinases (Ulk1, Ulk2), and autophagy receptors (Optineurin, Bnip3l).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Enriched functional pathways not previously implicated in Mtb pathogenesis include nucleocytoplasmic transport (p=1.92×10−19) and response to DNA damage (p=2.08×10−18).
claims.source: We identified other enriched functional pathways not previously implicated in Mtb pathogenesis such as nucleocytoplasmic transport and response to DNA damage (p=1.92×10−19, p=2.08×10−18; Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Protein abundance changes clustered into two large groups and several smaller clusters.
claims.source: Protein abundance changes clustered into two large groups and several smaller clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The group of proteins that increased in abundance during Mtb infection was functionally enriched for inflammatory, antiviral, and 'response to bacterium' pathways.
claims.source: The group of proteins that increased in abundance during Mtb infection was functionally enriched for inflammatory, antiviral, and 'response to bacterium', suggestive they are predominantly targets of TLR signaling (i.e., TLR2, NOS2, Il1b, FCGR4; Figure 3—figure supplement 2; p=2.19×10−13, 2.51 × 10−25, 8.32 × 10−15).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: OASL1 had the fourth greatest fold change among all non-imputed proteins that changed in abundance (34-fold change, p=1.56×10−12).
claims.source: Strikingly, among all of the non-imputed proteins that changed in abundance, OASL1 had the fourth greatest fold change (Figure 3A; 34-fold change, p=1.56×10−12), and there was also a large increase in OASL1 mRNA at the same time point (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Murine OASL1 downregulates the type I IFN response by binding to and inhibiting translation of IRF7 mRNA.
claims.source: While OAS proteins activate cleavage of viral nucleic acid (Choi et al., 2015), murine OASL1 downregulates the type I IFN response by binding to and inhibiting translation of IRF7 mRNA (Lee et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Choi et al., 2015 and Lee et al., 2013.

claims.claim: OASL1 mRNA was increased in macrophages infected with a hypervirulent Mtb strain.
claims.source: OASL1 regulation of the type I IFN response may play a critical role in Mtb pathogenesis as OASL1 mRNA was recently described to be increased in macrophages infected with a hypervirulent Mtb strain (Leisching et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Leisching et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The second cluster of proteins decreased in abundance and included ribosome biogenesis and DNA replication pathways (p=8.92×10−10, 8.32 × 10−11).
claims.source: The second cluster of proteins decreased in abundance and included ribosome biogenesis and DNA replication pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; p=8.92×10−10, 8.32 × 10−11), consistent with studies indicating that Mtb infection may arrest macrophage growth (Cumming et al., 2017), a strategy utilized by the intracellular pathogen Legionella pneumophila (Moss et al., 2019; Sol et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, and is supported by citations to Cumming et al., 2017; Moss et al., 2019; Sol et al., 2019.

claims.claim: There was a statistically significant increase in the autophagy receptors p62 and TAX1BP1 during Mtb infection.
claims.source: Although the autophagy pathway was not significantly enriched in our abundance data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), there was a statistically significant increase in the autophagy receptors p62 and TAX1BP1 during Mtb infection (Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Ubiquitylated substrates clustered into four classes during the 24 hr time course.
claims.source: During the 24 hr time course, ubiquitylated substrates clustered into four classes: 1. Peptides that decreased in ubiquitylation during infection, 2. Peptides that had increased ubiquitylation early (2–4 hr) after infection, 3. Peptides that were ubiquitylated between 6–8 hr after infection, and 4. Peptides that were identified as ubiquitylated only at the 24 hr time point (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: Autophagy was enriched at the later time points of infection (class 3 and 4).
claims.source: Autophagy, for example, was enriched at the later time points of infection (class 3 and 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: An enrichment in histones was identified among the group of proteins with decreased ubiquitylation during Mtb infection (Class 1, p=1.82×10−7, 5.89 × 10−7).
claims.source: We also identified an enrichment in histones among the group of proteins with decreased ubiquitylation during Mtb infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 3; Class 1, p=1.82×10−7, 5.89 × 10−7), which is likely reflective of the dramatic changes in the transcriptional program of macrophages when they encounter bacteria (Zou and Mallampalli, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and is supported by a citation to Zou and Mallampalli, 2014.

claims.claim: Phosphorylated substrates clustered into four discrete classes.
claims.source: Phosphorylated substrates also clustered together into four discrete classes: 1. Proteins that increased early after infection, 2. Proteins that increased later after infection, 3. Proteins that decreased early after infection, and 4. Proteins that decreased late after infection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the cluster analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Actin cytoskeleton organization and small GTPase mediated signal transduction changed dramatically throughout the 24 hr time course of infection as they were significantly enriched in all of the phosphorylation clusters.
claims.source: This analysis revealed that actin cytoskeleton organization and small GTPase mediated signal transduction changed dramatically throughout the 24 hr time course of infection as they were significantly enriched in all of the clusters (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The PhosFate bioinformatic tool identified kinases expected to be activated during Mtb infection, including those involved in inflammatory (IKBKB) and stress responses (several MAP kinases) as well as type I IFN signaling (JAK/STATs).
claims.source: Importantly, this approach identified kinases expected to be activated during Mtb infection, including those involved in inflammatory (IKBKB) and stress responses (several MAP kinases) as well as type I IFN signaling (JAK/STATs).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the PhosFate analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: Potential decreased activity of several cyclin dependent kinases was noted, consistent with the finding that primary macrophages stop proliferating upon infection.
claims.source: Conversely, we also noted potential decreased activity of several cyclin dependent kinases, consistent with the finding that primary macrophages stop proliferating upon infection (Cumming et al., 2017; Figure 3—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the PhosFate analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A, and is supported by a citation to Cumming et al., 2017.

claims.claim: The autophagy pathway was prominently enriched in both PTM datasets.
claims.source: The autophagy pathway was prominently enriched in both PTM datasets (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 3), with a significant number of phosphorylation events that occurred on autophagy cargo receptors (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 3, and the data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Among the autophagy receptors, p62 had the greatest number of phosphorylated residues that changed during Mtb infection and was among the most highly modified proteins in the proteomics datasets.
claims.source: While both p62 and NDP52 have been linked to Mtb targeting to the autophagosome (Watson et al., 2012), we found that only p62 was modified. In fact, among the autophagy receptors, p62 had the greatest number of phosphorylated residues that changed during Mtb infection and was among the most highly modified proteins in our proteomics datasets.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2A and is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Novel p62 phosphosites were identified at Ser-28, Ser-320, and Ser-372.
claims.source: We identified many of the previously recognized p62 phosphosites, including Ser-152 in the RIPK1 domain and Ser-226 in the TRAF6-binding domain (Richter et al., 2016), but we have identified novel residues as well (Ser-28, Ser-320, Ser-372; Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B, and is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2016.

claims.claim: Four autophagy receptors (BNIP3L, Optineurin, FUNDC1, and TAX1BP1) were selectively modified upon Mtb infection.
claims.source: Four receptors (BNIP3L, Optineurin, FUNDC1, and TAX1BP1) were selectively modified upon Mtb infection; these modifications occurred in functional domains of these receptors (Figure 2B) and changed through the time course of infection (Figure 2A,C–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and 2C-G.

claims.claim: Colocalization of Mtb with NBR1, Optineurin, TAX1BP1 and p62 was detected.
claims.source: Importantly, we detected colocalization of Mtb with NBR1, Optineurin, TAX1BP1 and p62 (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Both NBR1 and TAX1BP1 localized to Mtb to a similar extent as p62, whereas colocalization with Optineurin was considerably less frequent.
claims.source: Quantification of the percent of Mtb-containing phagosomes that colocalized with each receptor revealed that both NBR1 and TAX1BP1 localized to a similar extent as p62, whereas colocalization with Optineurin was considerably less frequent.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the quantification shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The ~30% colocalization rate of Mtb with p62 is consistent with previous findings.
claims.source: The ~30% colocalization rate of Mtb with p62 is consistent with previous findings (Watson et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the quantification shown in Figure 4B and is supported by a citation to Watson et al., 2012.

claims.claim: Infected Tax1bp1-/- cells gave rise to significant increases in Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to infected wild-type macrophages.
claims.source: In contrast, infected Tax1bp1-/- cells gave rise to significant increases in Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to infected wild-type macrophages (Figure 5B), indicating that this receptor functions subsequent to p62 and the assembly of signaling complexes to the phagosome, similar to that observed with Salmonella eneterica (Tumbarello et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 5B, and is supported by a citation to Tumbarello et al., 2015.

claims.claim: p62-deficient macrophages showed decreased targeting of Mtb to ubiquitin (FK2) compared to wild-type cells.
claims.source: Similar to prior results showing that p62-deficient macrophages are impaired in the targeting of Shigella vacuolar remnants to ubiquitin (Dupont et al., 2009), we found decreased targeting of Mtb to ubiquitin (FK2) in p62-/- macrophages compared to wild-type cells, consistent with an early role for p62 in signal amplification required for full cargo ubiquitylation (Figure 5B; Peng et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 5B, and is supported by citations to Dupont et al., 2009 and Peng et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Infected Tax1bp1 edited macrophages displayed increased Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to macrophages transduced with scramble control guides.
claims.source: In concordance with our observations in cells harvested from Tax1bp1-/- knockout mice, infected Tax1bp1 edited macrophages displayed increased Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to macrophages transduced with scramble control guides (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In Tax1bp1 edited or targeted knockout macrophages, a slight yet significant decrease in colocalization with LC3 was observed during Mtb infection.
claims.source: However, during Mtb infection of Tax1bp1 edited or targeted knockout macrophages, we observed a slight yet significant decrease in colocalization with LC3 (Figure 6A and B) that persisted in the presence of interferon-γ (IFN-γ) stimulation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the microscopy data shown in Figure 6A, 6B, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: TAX1BP1 is required for efficient delivery of LC3-containing autophagosomal membranes to the Mtb containing phagosome.
claims.source: Taken together, these results indicate that TAX1BP1 functions in a specific step of autophagosomal targeting and is required for efficient delivery LC3-containing autophagosomal membranes to the Mtb containing phagosome.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the microscopy data shown in Figures 5 and 6.

claims.claim: A moderate yet statistically significant increase in Mtb CFUs was observed at 3- and 5 days post-infection in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages compared to wild-type controls.
claims.source: We observed a moderate yet statistically significant increase in Mtb CFUs at 3- and 5 days post-infection in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages compared to wild-type controls (Figure 6C).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the CFU data shown in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: Using a bioluminescent Mtb reporter strain at a multiplicity of infection of 2 or 5, bacterial growth was accelerated in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages.
claims.source: Likewise, using a bioluminescent Mtb reporter strain (Roberts et al., 2019) at a multiplicity of infection of 2 or 5, bacterial growth was similarly accelerated in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages (Figure 6D and E; Penn et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the luminescence data shown in Figure 6D and 6E, and is supported by citations to Roberts et al., 2019 and Penn et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Tax1bp1-/- macrophages were still capable of restricting Mtb growth when stimulated with IFN-γ.
claims.source: In contrast, Tax1bp1-/- macrophages were still capable of restricting Mtb growth when stimulated with IFN-γ, an effect likely due to production of normal levels of nitric oxide, the major anti-Mtb effector of murine macrophages induced by this cytokine (Figure 6E; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: In the absence of IFN-γ, TAX1BP1 deficiency leads to increased Mtb growth in macrophages ex vivo.
claims.source: These results reveal that, in the absence of IFN-γ, TAX1BP1 deficiency leads to increased Mtb growth in macrophages ex vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the growth data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claims.claim: Levels of secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-12, and TNF-α did not significantly change in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages.
claims.source: Although TAX1BP1 regulates NF-κB-mediated inflammation in some contexts (Iha et al., 2008), levels of secreted pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-6, IL-12, and TNF-α did not significantly change in these experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the cytokine data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and is supported by a citation to Iha et al., 2008.

claims.claim: A modest yet significant increase in the production of type I interferon was measured in Tax1bp1-/- macrophages, consistent with previous reports of TAX1BP1 action.
claims.source: However, we measured a modest yet significant increase in the production of type I interferon, a cytokine that promotes bacterial growth in vivo, consistent with previous reports of TAX1BP1 action (Parvatiyar et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the ISRE reporter data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B, and is supported by a citation to Parvatiyar et al., 2010.

claims.claim: The study generated a comprehensive database of changes in protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during Mtb infection of primary bone marrow-derived macrophages.
claims.source: In this study, we generated a comprehensive database of changes in protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation during Mtb infection of primary bone marrow-derived macrophages.
claims.evidence: This is a summary statement about the study's main output.

claims.claim: The thousands of PTM changes identified represent an ensemble of the various pathways that are integrated to meet the challenge of infection, but also reflect the pathogenic strategies of Mtb.
claims.source: We envision that the thousands of PTM changes we have identified represents an ensemble of the various pathways that are integrated to meet the challenge of infection, but also reflect the pathogenic strategies of Mtb.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: The analysis revealed changes in macrophage functional pathways not previously known to play a role during infection such as mRNA metabolism and DNA replication.
claims.source: In addition to these host pathways, our analysis also revealed changes in macrophage functional pathways not previously known to play a role during infection such as mRNA metabolism and DNA replication, highlighting potential areas of new biology involved in the host response to Mtb.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: Autophagy receptor phosphorylation, including TAX1BP1, was greatest between the two peaks of overall host protein phosphorylation (6–8 hr).
claims.source: In contrast to the bimodal peak in overall host protein phosphorylation early (2–4 hr) and late (24 hr) after infection, autophagy receptor phosphorylation, including TAX1BP1, was greatest in between these two peaks (6–8 hr).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2C-G.

claims.claim: Dephosphorylation of two residues in the BH3 domain of BNIP3L (Ser-141 and Ser-144) was found during Mtb infection.
claims.source: We found Mtb infection elicited post-translational modifications in several autophagy receptors including dephosphorylation of two residues in the BH3 domain of BNIP3L (Figure 2B E), an atypical BH3-only protein involved in mitochondrial clearance (Novak et al., 2010) and cell death (Imazu et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B and 2E, and is supported by citations to Novak et al., 2010 and Imazu et al., 1999.

claims.claim: Novel phosphosites in FUNDC1 (Tyr-11) and Optineurin (Thr-210, Thr-212, and Ser-556) were identified.
claims.source: Our phosphoproteomic analysis also identified new phosphosites in FUNDC1 (Tyr-11) and Optineurin. While affinity purification of GFP-tagged optineurin previously revealed TBK1-mediated phosphorylation at residues adjacent to the LIR and UBAN domains of Optineurin (Richter et al., 2016), we found two novel phosphosites between its LIR and coiled coil domains at Thr-210 and Thr-212, in addition to a phosphosite at Ser-556 in its zinc finger domain (Figure 2B–G).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B-G, and is supported by a citation to Richter et al., 2016.

claims.claim: p62 protein abundance and ubiquitylation increased during Mtb infection.
claims.source: In addition to undergoing extensive phosphorylation, p62 protein abundance and ubiquitylation increased during Mtb infection (Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: A novel ubiquitylation site in the p62 dimerization domain at Lys-13 was discovered during Mtb infection.
claims.source: While ubiquitylation of human p62 at Lys-157 has been previously reported in HEK293T (Peng et al., 2017) and SUMOylation of human p62 at Lys-437 was discovered in HeLa and U2OS cell lines (Hendriks et al., 2017), we discovered a third lysine residue ubiquitylated in the dimerization domain during Mtb infection (Lys-13) which has not been described previously.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data from the study, and is supported by citations to Peng et al., 2017 and Hendriks et al., 2017.

claims.claim: p62-deficient macrophages were unable to recruit ubiquitin to Mtb, supporting a model whereby p62 recruitment leads to a feed forward loop with further recruitment of ubiquitin to the autophagosome.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that p62-deficient macrophages were unable to recruit ubiquitin to Mtb, supporting a model whereby p62 recruitment leads to a feed forward loop with further recruitment of ubiquitin to the autophagosome (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 5B and the model shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: TAX1BP1 was phosphorylated during Mtb infection, and its protein abundance also increased.
claims.source: Finally, the autophagy receptor, TAX1BP1, was phosphorylated during Mtb infection, and its protein abundance also increased (Figure 2B; Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data shown in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: TAX1BP1 functions at a step downstream of p62, ubiquitin, and phospho-TBK1 recruitment, enabling full maturation of the ubiquitylated Mtb phagosome to a LC3-positive phagophore.
claims.source: In contrast to p62's function in recruiting ubiquitin to the Mtb autophagosome, TAX1BP1 appears to function at a step downstream of p62, ubiquitin, and phospho-TBK1 recruitment, enabling full maturation of the ubiquitylated Mtb phagosome to a LC3-positive phagophore (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data shown in Figures 5 and 6, and is illustrated in the model shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: TAX1BP1 is not required for global autophagy in T cells or MEFs.
claims.source: Intriguingly, TAX1BP1 is not required for global autophagy in T cells or MEFs (Whang et al., 2017), indicating that TAX1BP1 may play a role in autophagy of select cargos.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Whang et al., 2017.

claims.claim: TAX1BP1 has been implicated as an autophagy receptor important for clearance of Salmonella in a manner that requires myosin VI.
claims.source: However, TAX1BP1 has been implicated as an autophagy receptor important for clearance of Salmonella in a manner that requires myosin VI, one of TAX1BP1's binding partners (Tumbarello et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tumbarello et al., 2015.

claims.claim: TAX1BP1 was originally identified as an A20-binding protein.
claims.source: Originally identified as an A20-binding protein (Heyninck et al., 1999), TAX1BP1 activates this ubiquitin editing enzyme to downregulate inflammatory responses by inhibiting TNF-α and IL-1β-induced NF-kB activation (Iha et al., 2008; Shembade et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heyninck et al., 1999; Iha et al., 2008; Shembade et al., 2011.

claims.claim: Increased TAX1BP1 phosphorylation at Ser-693, a substrate for IKKα, was identified during infection.
claims.source: Given that hyperinflammatory responses promote Mtb infection (Olive and Sassetti, 2018), we reasoned TAX1BP1 may also function to limit these responses, especially since we identified increased TAX1BP1 phosphorylation at Ser-693, a substrate for IKKα, during infection.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on the data from the study, and is supported by a citation to Olive and Sassetti, 2018.

claims.claim: The mass spectrometry proteomics RAW mass spectrum files and all database searches have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD015361.
claims.source: The mass spectrometry proteomics RAW mass spectrum files and all database searches have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE (Perez-Riverol et al., 2019; Deutsch et al., 2017) partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD015361.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about data availability, supported by citations to Perez-Riverol et al., 2019 and Deutsch et al., 2017.

results.result: The manuscript provides background context on Mtb as a successful human pathogen causing chronic infections, with macrophages playing a central role in pathogenesis. The interactions between Mtb and macrophages have coevolved over ~70,000 years, and nearly 10 million people develop tuberculosis annually.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 are well-supported by established knowledge and appropriate citations (Russell 2011, Comas et al. 2013, WHO 2018). These are standard background statements in the tuberculosis field that accurately represent the current understanding of Mtb pathogenesis and epidemiology.

results.result: The manuscript describes established mechanisms of Mtb-macrophage interactions, including TLR2 engagement, phagosomal maturation arrest via ESX-1, membrane perforation leading to cGAS/STING/TBK1 activation and type I IFN response, and activation of ubiquitin-mediated selective autophagy. The role of canonical autophagy in antimicrobial effects remains unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C14 accurately summarize well-established prior work on Mtb pathogenesis with appropriate citations (Gopalakrishnan & Salgame 2016, Sturgill-Koszycki et al. 1994, MacGurn & Cox 2007, Watson et al. 2015, etc.). These background claims provide necessary context for the current study and acknowledge areas of ongoing uncertainty (C9, C14).

results.result: The manuscript establishes the rationale for PTM analysis by noting that prior global approaches relied on mRNA profiling, which has limitations. PTM analysis provides more comprehensive assessment of cellular state during infection, as many pathways including autophagy are regulated by PTMs rather than transcription. Some autophagy components and receptors have been implicated in Mtb infection, but many remain untested.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C23 provide well-supported rationale for the study approach, citing appropriate literature (Ehrt et al. 2001, Lamark et al. 2017, Herhaus & Dikic 2015, Watson et al. 2012, Manzanillo et al. 2013, Franco et al. 2017). The logic that PTM analysis captures biological processes not reflected in mRNA changes is sound and supported by established knowledge of cellular regulation.

results.result: The study used mass spectrometry to analyze changes in protein abundance, phosphorylation, and ubiquitylation in primary murine macrophages infected with Mtb over a 24-hour time course with biological triplicates. Mock infections were performed at 0, 6, and 24 hours, with minimal changes between uninfected timepoints. Technical and biological replicates showed high reproducibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C24, C28-C31 describe the experimental design and data quality. The approach is sound with appropriate biological replicates (n=3), time-matched controls, and demonstrated reproducibility (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1). The finding of minimal changes in mock-infected cells (C30, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C) validates the experimental system.

results.result: The study identified over 1000 statistically significant changes in protein abundance or PTMs during Mtb infection. Changes in protein abundance and ubiquitylation progressively increased over time, while phosphopeptide changes showed a bimodal pattern with peaks at early (2-4 hr) and late (24 hr) timepoints.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C32-C34 are supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplements 2-3. The temporal dynamics are clearly demonstrated, with appropriate statistical analysis (p<0.05, log2-fold-change ≥1 or ≤-1). The bimodal phosphorylation pattern (C34) is a novel observation that distinguishes phosphorylation dynamics from other PTMs.

results.result: Correlation analysis between mRNA and protein changes revealed weak correlation at 6 hours (ρ=0.36) but stronger correlation at 24 hours (ρ=0.74). However, poor correlations were observed between mRNA and phosphorylated (ρ=0.37) or ubiquitylated proteins (ρ=0.52) at 24 hours, indicating that PTM-controlled processes operate independently of transcriptional changes.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C38 are well-supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 1D-F and Figure 1—figure supplement 4, with comparison to published RNAseq data (Braverman et al. 2016). The interpretation (C38) that PTMs capture biology independent of gene expression is justified by the data and consistent with prior work (Berg-Larsen et al. 2013). The correlation values are clearly stated and appropriately interpreted.

results.result: During Mtb infection, 470 proteins changed significantly in abundance, 1489 in phosphorylation, and 606 in ubiquitylation, with limited overlap between the three categories.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C42 are supported by the Venn diagram analysis in Figure 3B. The numbers are clearly stated and the limited overlap demonstrates that different PTMs capture distinct aspects of the cellular response. This finding reinforces the value of measuring multiple PTM types simultaneously.

results.result: Pathway enrichment analysis revealed highly significant enrichment of antiviral responses (p=4.53×10⁻²⁰), small GTPase-mediated signal transduction (p=2.12×10⁻²⁶), regulation of catabolic processes including autophagy (p=2.39×10⁻²⁵), and previously unimplicated pathways including nucleocytoplasmic transport (p=1.92×10⁻¹⁹) and DNA damage response (p=2.08×10⁻¹⁸).
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by pathway enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, with highly significant p-values. The identification of expected pathways (antiviral, GTPase signaling, autophagy) validates the approach, while novel pathways (nucleocytoplasmic transport, DNA damage) represent new findings. The analysis used appropriate bioinformatics tools (Metascape) with GO Biological Processes.

results.result: Temporal clustering analysis of protein abundance changes revealed two major clusters: proteins that increased (enriched for inflammatory, antiviral, and bacterial response pathways) and proteins that decreased (enriched for ribosome biogenesis and DNA replication). OASL1 showed the fourth greatest fold change (34-fold, p=1.56×10⁻¹²) and may regulate type I IFN responses. Autophagy receptors p62 and TAX1BP1 increased significantly.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C53 are supported by cluster analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and abundance data in Supplementary file 3. The functional enrichments are statistically significant and biologically interpretable. The OASL1 finding (C49-C51) is notable and supported by both proteomics and transcriptomics data (Figure 3A, Figure 1D), with appropriate citations to prior work on OASL1 function (Lee et al. 2013, Leisching et al. 2017).

results.result: Temporal clustering of PTM changes revealed distinct patterns: ubiquitylated substrates clustered into four classes with autophagy enriched at later timepoints (6-24 hr) and histones showing decreased ubiquitylation (p=1.82×10⁻⁷). Phosphorylated substrates also formed four classes, with actin cytoskeleton organization and small GTPase signaling enriched across all clusters.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by cluster analyses in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 3. The temporal patterns are clearly demonstrated with appropriate statistical support. The finding that actin cytoskeleton and GTPase signaling are dynamically regulated throughout infection (C58) is consistent with the known importance of these pathways in Mtb pathogenesis.

results.result: PhosFate bioinformatic analysis predicted activation of expected kinases (IKBKB, MAP kinases, JAK/STATs) and decreased activity of cyclin-dependent kinases, consistent with macrophage growth arrest during infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C60 are supported by PhosFate analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A. The identification of expected kinases validates the computational approach, while the CDK prediction (C60) is consistent with prior observations (Cumming et al. 2017). However, these are predictions that would require experimental validation for definitive confirmation.

results.result: Autophagy pathway was prominently enriched in PTM datasets, with p62 showing the greatest number of phosphorylation changes among autophagy receptors, including novel sites at Ser-28, Ser-320, and Ser-372. Four autophagy receptors (BNIP3L, Optineurin, FUNDC1, TAX1BP1) were selectively modified in functional domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C64 are supported by data in Figure 2A-B and Figure 3C. The identification of novel p62 phosphosites (C63) is supported by comparison with known sites (Richter et al. 2016). The finding that multiple autophagy receptors are modified (C64, Figure 2B, 2C-G) is a key discovery that motivated subsequent functional studies. The modifications occur in functional domains, suggesting biological relevance.

results.result: Microscopy analysis revealed that NBR1, Optineurin, TAX1BP1, and p62 colocalize with Mtb during infection. NBR1 and TAX1BP1 showed similar colocalization rates to p62 (~30%), while Optineurin colocalization was less frequent (~7%).
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C67 are supported by microscopy data in Figure 4A-B. The quantification is based on appropriate image analysis (45 images per coverslip, three technical replicates). The ~30% p62 colocalization rate (C67) is consistent with prior findings (Watson et al. 2012), validating the experimental approach. The identification of TAX1BP1 as a novel Mtb-colocalizing receptor is a key finding.

results.result: Tax1bp1-/- macrophages showed significantly increased Mtb colocalization with ubiquitin, phospho-TBK1, and p62 compared to wild-type cells, while p62-/- macrophages showed decreased ubiquitin targeting to Mtb. Similar results were obtained with CRISPR-edited Tax1bp1 macrophages.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C70 are supported by microscopy data in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1. The use of both knockout mice and CRISPR editing (C70) provides orthogonal validation. The automated colocalization analysis from >1000 infected cells provides robust quantification. Statistical significance is demonstrated (p<0.001). The contrasting phenotypes of Tax1bp1-/- and p62-/- cells support distinct roles in the autophagy pathway.

results.result: Tax1bp1-/- or CRISPR-edited macrophages showed a slight but significant decrease in Mtb colocalization with LC3, persisting even with IFN-γ stimulation. This indicates TAX1BP1 is required for efficient delivery of LC3-containing autophagosomal membranes to the Mtb phagosome.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C72 are supported by microscopy data in Figure 6A-B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1. The decrease in LC3 colocalization is statistically significant (p<0.05) and observed in both knockout and CRISPR-edited cells. The persistence with IFN-γ stimulation (C71) indicates the defect is not overcome by immune activation. The interpretation (C72) is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanism remains to be fully elucidated.

results.result: Tax1bp1-/- macrophages showed moderate but statistically significant increases in Mtb CFUs at 3 and 5 days post-infection and accelerated bacterial growth measured by bioluminescence at MOI 2 or 5. However, Tax1bp1-/- macrophages retained the ability to restrict Mtb growth when stimulated with IFN-γ, indicating TAX1BP1 deficiency leads to increased Mtb growth in the absence of IFN-γ.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C76 are supported by CFU data (Figure 6C) and bioluminescence assays (Figure 6D-E). The growth phenotype is modest but statistically significant and reproducible across two independent assays. The rescue by IFN-γ (C75, Figure 6E) is consistent with normal nitric oxide production (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and indicates TAX1BP1 functions in a parallel antimicrobial pathway. The interpretation (C76) is well-supported by the data.

results.result: Tax1bp1-/- macrophages showed no significant changes in pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-6, IL-12, TNF-α) but exhibited a modest yet significant increase in type I interferon production, consistent with previous reports of TAX1BP1 function.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C78 are supported by cytokine measurements in Figure 6—figure supplement 2. The lack of change in pro-inflammatory cytokines (C77) argues against a general inflammatory defect, while the increased type I IFN (C78) is consistent with prior work (Parvatiyar et al. 2010) and may contribute to the growth phenotype since type I IFN promotes Mtb growth in vivo.

results.result: The study generated a comprehensive database of PTM changes during Mtb infection, representing an ensemble of host responses and pathogenic strategies. The analysis revealed changes in previously unrecognized pathways including mRNA metabolism and DNA replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 accurately summarize the study's main contribution. The database is comprehensive (>1000 significant changes) and publicly available (PXD015361, C94). The identification of novel pathways (C81) is supported by enrichment analysis (Figure 3). Claim C80 is somewhat speculative but represents a reasonable interpretation of the data.

results.result: Autophagy receptor phosphorylation peaked at 6-8 hours, between the bimodal peaks of overall phosphorylation. Novel PTMs were identified including BNIP3L dephosphorylation at Ser-141/144, FUNDC1 phosphorylation at Tyr-11, Optineurin phosphorylation at Thr-210/212 and Ser-556, and p62 ubiquitylation at Lys-13.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C86 are supported by temporal analysis (Figure 2C-G) and domain mapping (Figure 2B). The identification of novel PTM sites is based on comparison with published data (Richter et al. 2016, Peng et al. 2017, Hendriks et al. 2017). The temporal dynamics of autophagy receptor modification (C82) represent a novel finding that distinguishes these proteins from bulk phosphorylation patterns.

results.result: p62-deficient macrophages were unable to recruit ubiquitin to Mtb, supporting a feed-forward loop model. TAX1BP1 was phosphorylated and increased in abundance during infection, and functions downstream of p62, ubiquitin, and phospho-TBK1 recruitment to enable maturation of the ubiquitylated Mtb phagosome to an LC3-positive phagophore.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 integrate multiple lines of evidence (Figures 5B, 2B, Supplementary file 4, Figure 7 model). The p62 feed-forward loop model (C87) is supported by the ubiquitin recruitment defect and is consistent with prior work (Dupont et al. 2009, Peng et al. 2017). The TAX1BP1 functional model (C89) is well-supported by the sequential accumulation of ubiquitin/p62/pTBK1 but decreased LC3 in Tax1bp1-/- cells, indicating a block at a specific step.

results.result: TAX1BP1 is not required for global autophagy but has been implicated in selective autophagy of Salmonella. TAX1BP1 was originally identified as an A20-binding protein that regulates NF-κB signaling. Increased TAX1BP1 phosphorylation at Ser-693, an IKKα substrate, was identified during Mtb infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 provide important context for TAX1BP1 function, supported by appropriate citations (Whang et al. 2017, Tumbarello et al. 2015, Heyninck et al. 1999, Iha et al. 2008, Shembade et al. 2011, Olive & Sassetti 2018). The Ser-693 phosphorylation (C93) is a novel finding from the current study that may link TAX1BP1 to inflammatory signaling, though the functional significance was not fully explored.

results.result: The mass spectrometry data have been deposited to ProteomeXchange/PRIDE with identifier PXD015361.
results.evaluation: Claim C94 documents appropriate data deposition, making the resource publicly available. This is essential for reproducibility and enables the community to mine the dataset for additional insights.
